title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
authors: Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram, B. Pabitramohan Prusty, Rohit Batra
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

infographic.key_insight: This review traces how materials information extraction has evolved from rule-based pipelines to multimodal LLMs and agentic systems that support materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated literature extraction can populate materials databases and knowledge graphs, assist researchers, and support closed-loop discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories.
method: Review rule-based, NLP, transformer-encoder, LLM, and agentic extraction approaches.
Examine extraction across text, tables, and figures.
Assess generated datasets, extraction accuracy, computational costs, and pipeline design.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a critical assessment of datasets, accuracy, and costs but reports no quantitative results and highlights scarce reliable benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable sample-level linkage of structure, properties, processing, and performance remains an open challenge, compounded by inconsistent terminology across document modalities.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
authors: Yue Wu, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

infographic.key_insight: Retention-constrained fine-tuning improves an aluminium MACE potential’s defect predictions while preserving its tested near-equilibrium mechanical and vibrational response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The protocol supports more reliable atomistic simulations of aluminium defect dynamics and plasticity without sacrificing validated bulk behavior.
method: Select configurations using force uncertainty from sensitivities over 144 readout weights, updating covariance within each batch.
Iteratively update all model parameters while anchoring historical relative energies.
Gate model acceptance against historical elastic-group energy and vibrational tolerances.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 32 acquisitions and 400 gradient updates, mean development force error fell from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Å, outperforming sampling baselines; all three force-uncertainty runs met retention criteria, with harmonic phonon RMS drift below 0.05 THz.
infographic.watch_item: Retention is demonstrated only for the tested aluminium configurations and tolerances; broader deployment requires additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity

title: Phase field dislocation dynamics prediction of stacking fault widths in Cu-Al Alloys using generalised stacking fault energy from DFT and interatomic potentials
authors: Arjun Varma R., Ankosh D. Deshmukh, Sushil Kumar, Vaishali Shah, M. P. Gururajan
abstract: The equilibrium width of intrinsic stacking faults is an important material parameter affecting key deformation phenomena. Here, we perform a comparative assessment of $γ$-surfaces generated using MD -- with a classical embedded-atom potential (ZW) and a machine-learned Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) -- and density functional theory (DFT), for Cu-Al alloys of varying Al content, and incorporate them as an energy term in PFDD simulations to obtain the equilibrium SFW. All three methods reproduce the lattice parameter and elastic moduli of Cu and Cu-Al alloys in reasonable agreement with each other and with experimental measurements from literature, but the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces, for both ZW and GAP, deviate substantially from DFT at the seven characteristic points, with the largest discrepancies at $T$ and $T_1$. When incorporated into PFDD, the DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces successfully predict an equilibrium SFW that increases with Al content and agrees well with standalone MD measurements and experimental values for pure Cu, whereas the MD-derived $γ$-surfaces do not yield an accurate SFW within PFDD, as the altered generalized stacking fault energy landscape causes the dissociating partials to become pinned soon after separation. These results show that DFT-derived $γ$-surfaces remain the more reliable route to alloy SFW prediction, and interatomic potentials must capture the shear path accurately to enable robust, efficient MD-PFDD modelling of stacking faults in alloys.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-derived stacking-fault energy surfaces enable reliable PFDD predictions of widening stacking faults with increasing Al content, while surfaces from both tested interatomic potentials cause premature partial-dislocation pinning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate alloy deformation modelling requires interatomic potentials that reproduce the shear-energy landscape, not just lattice parameters and elastic moduli.
method: Generate Cu–Al generalized stacking-fault energy surfaces using DFT, embedded-atom ZW and machine-learned GAP potentials.
Incorporate each energy surface into phase field dislocation dynamics (PFDD) simulations to predict equilibrium stacking-fault widths.
Compare energy landscapes and predicted widths with standalone MD results and available experimental values.
infographic.evidence_signal: Despite reasonable agreement in lattice parameters and elastic moduli, both potential-derived surfaces differ substantially from DFT at seven characteristic points; DFT-based widths agree well with standalone MD measurements and experimental values for pure Cu.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental width agreement is reported for pure Cu; validation across alloy compositions remains important before broader engineering use.
infographic.paper_title: Phase field dislocation dynamics prediction of stacking fault widths in Cu-Al Alloys using generalised stacking fault energy from DFT and interatomic potentials

title: From Autonomous Knowledge Generation to Generalizable Property Prediction: A Precision-First Pipeline for Electro-Optic Materials Discovery
authors: Dibakar Datta
abstract: Electro-optic materials, whose refractive index changes linearly with an applied electric field (the Pockels effect), set the speed and energy of optical modulators and microwave-to-optical links for quantum computing. Designing better materials requires optimizing composition alongside temperature, strain, and bias field. However, general repositories lack electro-optic tensor data. We present a pipeline that builds such a database from literature following the rule: "no value is better than a wrong value." The pipeline has five stages: physics-aware acquisition, layout-aware extraction via LLM and deterministic table parsers, a three-tier verification gate, cross-paper consensus using median and median absolute deviation, and a noise-robust surrogate model audited by leave-one-material-out (LOMO) testing. Physics enters directly: notation is mapped, point-group symmetry-forbidden Pockels components are rejected, equivalent labels are merged, and values carry provenance tags. In a run over 49 publications, the gate processed 816 candidates into 414 accepted, 215 held for review, and 187 rejected. Against a hand-certified gold standard of 303 values from 16 papers, the run achieved a precision of 0.51 and recall of 0.48 for exact record matches. Across four database snapshots, held-out materials where the surrogate model beat a predict-the-mean baseline grew from 1 of 4 to 9 of 13 as the database expanded from 10 to 22 materials. While not a controlled comparison, this trend supports the premise that a precision-oriented, physics-checked database can power forward models beyond its training set and clarifies requirements for inverse material design.

infographic.key_insight: A precision-first, physics-checked literature pipeline builds electro-optic property datasets that support prediction for materials excluded from training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could guide electro-optic material selection for optical modulators and microwave-to-optical quantum links across composition and operating conditions.
method: Acquire relevant literature and extract values using layout-aware LLMs and deterministic table parsers.
Apply three-tier verification, normalize notation, reject symmetry-forbidden components, and retain provenance.
Consolidate cross-paper values using median and median absolute deviation, then audit a noise-robust surrogate with leave-one-material-out testing.
infographic.evidence_signal: From 49 papers, 414 of 816 candidates were accepted; exact-match precision/recall were 0.51/0.48 against 303 certified values, while held-out baseline wins rose from 1/4 to 9/13 as coverage grew from 10 to 22 materials.
infographic.watch_item: Exact-record accuracy remains modest, and the uncontrolled database-growth comparison does not establish that curation caused improved generalization.
infographic.paper_title: From Autonomous Knowledge Generation to Generalizable Property Prediction: A Precision-First Pipeline for Electro-Optic Materials Discovery

title: No Value Is Better Than a Wrong Value: Finding and Handling Erroneous Data in Literature-Mined Datasets for AI
authors: Achyut Manoj, Advai Aiyer, Andrew Lee, Nayan Saini, Pragya Birla, Dibakar Datta
abstract: Machine learning across materials science, chemistry, energy, and medicine increasingly relies on literature-extracted datasets due to a lack of curated databases. However, automated extraction introduces errors: text recognition misreads digits, units and notations are confused, values are misattributed, and LLMs hallucinate numbers. Drawing on our work building an electro-optic property database, we present a taxonomy of errors organized by their origin and signatures, alongside a layered framework for error detection. The framework combines schema and provenance checks, physical admissibility (bounds, symmetry, and governing equations), cross-source statistical consensus, model auditing, and suspicion-ranked review. In a production run, our verification gate halted 402 of 816 candidate values with typed reasons. Yet, an audit against curated references showed that 30 of 112 accepted values were defective; standard symmetry rules alone caught 21 of these. On measured BaTiO3 and KNbO3 tensors, constitutive identities caught 8 of 10 single-value errors and isolated the corrupted entries. In a controlled benchmark, the combined framework caught 81% of errors at 85% precision, including errors in single-report materials, bringing model accuracy on held-out data to within 3% of a model trained on clean data. Uncleaned data severely impairs discovery: 89% of the twenty largest values were errors, causing AI searches to prioritize false positives. Once bad numbers are controlled, missing measurement conditions emerge as the main limit, as distinct records become indistinguishable without full context. We outline directions for the field, including shared physics rule libraries and self-reporting databases.

infographic.key_insight: Rejecting suspect literature-mined values using physics-aware checks can protect materials AI from errors that distort discovery rankings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Materials-data pipelines should validate provenance, physical consistency, and cross-source agreement before extracted values enter predictive models.
method: Classify extraction errors by origin and observable signatures.
Layer schema and provenance checks with physical bounds, symmetry rules, and governing equations.
Combine cross-source consensus and model auditing to prioritize suspicious records for review.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a controlled benchmark, the combined framework detected 81% of errors at 85% precision and brought held-out model accuracy within 3% of a model trained on clean data.
infographic.watch_item: Validation remains imperfect: 30 of 112 accepted values were defective in a curated-reference audit, and missing measurement conditions limit record comparability.
infographic.paper_title: No Value Is Better Than a Wrong Value: Finding and Handling Erroneous Data in Literature-Mined Datasets for AI

title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials
authors: Sarath Menon, Braulio Sanchez Ortega, Ralf Drautz
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations with near \textit{ab initio} accuracy over large length and time scales. Foundation models extend this capability across the periodic table but inherit the thermodynamic description of the electronic structure methods used to generate their training data. Small errors in relative phase stability can therefore produce large errors in transformation temperatures. We introduce an additive thermodynamic correction layer that shifts phase free energies towards an assessed reference without retraining or modifying the base potential. A first order thermodynamic construction converts the required phase free energy shifts directly into configuration energy targets, which are fitted using a linear atomic cluster expansion and refined iteratively from measured free energies. We apply the method to melting and solid to solid transformations across elements with different crystal structures using a foundation GRACE model. After the correction, all transformation temperatures lie within the prescribed tolerance of the assessed values, including Ca, Ti, and Zr, where a solid to solid transition and melting are corrected together. Static energy curves, bulk moduli, and liquid structure remain close to those of the base model. Vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density depend on the corrected phase balance and change where the correction is large. The method requires neither retraining, differentiable dynamics, nor access to the parameters of the base potential. It provides a modular route for combining transferable atomistic models with assessed phase thermodynamics.

infographic.key_insight: An additive thermodynamic correction layer aligns machine learning interatomic potentials with assessed phase thermodynamics without retraining the base model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables more accurate melting and solid–solid transformation predictions while retaining transferable atomistic models.
method: Convert required phase free-energy shifts into configuration energy targets using a first-order thermodynamic construction.
Fit an additive linear atomic cluster expansion correction.
Refine the correction iteratively using measured free energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests with a foundation GRACE model brought all evaluated transformation temperatures within prescribed tolerances, including simultaneous solid–solid and melting corrections for Ca, Ti, and Zr.
infographic.watch_item: Large corrections can alter vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density, so these properties require validation.
infographic.paper_title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials

title: Exploring Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Representation Learning of Powder X-ray Diffraction Patterns
authors: Ming-Chiang Chang, Brian DeCost
abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the primary high-throughput method for resolving crystal structures, a cornerstone of materials science. As high-throughput synthesis and self-driving laboratories advance, automated XRD pattern analysis has become vital for accelerating materials discovery. However, traditional matrix factorization methods fail when lattice variations cause non-linear peak shifts. At the same time, supervised learning approaches face a combinatorial explosion when handling multi-phase mixtures. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to learn representation embeddings from 1D diffraction patterns. By optimizing a masked self-prediction loss directly within the latent space, the framework captures high-level crystallographic semantics. Downstream evaluations show that lightweight attentive probes trained on frozen JEPA representations achieve space group classification and lattice parameter estimation accuracy close to much larger supervised vision transformers. Furthermore, latent probing reveals that the learned representation space naturally organizes physical transformations, isolating smooth trajectories for peak broadening. Interestingly, decoding along latent paths between single-phase crystal representations yields realistic multi-phase mixture patterns, demonstrating an emergent continuous structure learned without explicit multi-phase supervision.

infographic.key_insight: Self-supervised JEPA embeddings capture crystallographic structure in powder XRD patterns and show emergent representations of peak broadening and multi-phase mixtures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Frozen JEPA representations could support automated XRD analysis in high-throughput materials workflows with lightweight task-specific probes.
method: Learn embeddings from 1D diffraction patterns using a Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture.
Optimize masked self-prediction directly in latent space.
Evaluate frozen representations with lightweight attentive probes and latent-space decoding.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports space group classification and lattice parameter estimation accuracy close to much larger supervised vision transformers, plus realistic mixture patterns decoded along latent paths between single-phase representations.
infographic.watch_item: Realistic decoded mixtures do not establish reliable phase identification or quantification on experimental multi-phase XRD data.
infographic.paper_title: Exploring Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Representation Learning of Powder X-ray Diffraction Patterns

title: Transition Metal-Anchored Newly Synthesized Aza-Triphenylene Monolayer for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction: Insights from DFT
authors: Soumendra Kumar Das, Jagannath Pradhan, Prasanjit Samal, Sridhar Sahu, Brahmananda Chakraborty
abstract: First-principles calculations were employed to explore the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity in two-dimensional aza-triphenylene monolayers functionalized with transition metals. Among the various metals studied, Co, Ru, and Y demonstrate outstanding catalytic efficacy, lowering the hydrogen adsorption free energy from -0.78 eV for pure aza-triphenylene to 0.05, 0.20, and 0.06 eV, respectively. Volcano plot analysis corroborates their enhanced HER activity. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations confirm thermal stability, while the electronic structure and charge transfer analysis reveal the strong catalyst-surface interaction. Metal decoration also improves the carrier mobility, particularly for Ru-functionalized aza-triphenylene. The climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for Co-functionalized aza-triphenylene exhibit activation barriers of 1.61, 2.29, and 5.88 eV for the Volmer, Heyrovsky, and Tafel reactions, respectively, highlighting a preferred Volmer-Heyrovsky route with the Heyrovsky being the rate-determining step. These findings highlight the potential of transition-metal-functionalized aza-triphenylene as a promising platform for developing efficient HER electrocatalysts.

infographic.key_insight: DFT predicts that Co, Ru, and Y anchoring tunes aza-triphenylene toward favorable hydrogen adsorption for hydrogen evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Metal-functionalized aza-triphenylene offers a computationally identified platform for designing two-dimensional HER electrocatalysts.
method: First-principles adsorption energetics and HER volcano analysis
Ab initio molecular dynamics and electronic-structure analysis
Climbing-image nudged elastic band reaction-path calculations
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted hydrogen adsorption free energies shift from −0.78 eV for pristine aza-triphenylene to 0.05, 0.20, and 0.06 eV with Co, Ru, and Y, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental HER performance remains unverified, and the predicted 2.29 eV Heyrovsky barrier for Co indicates a substantial kinetic limitation despite favorable adsorption.
infographic.paper_title: Transition Metal-Anchored Newly Synthesized Aza-Triphenylene Monolayer for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution Reaction: Insights from DFT

title: TCSP3.0: Template-Based Crystal Structure Prediction with Coefficient-Preserving Element Substitution and Structural Diversity
authors: Ying Feng, Jeffrey Hu, Lai Wei, Liang Tao, Madeline Miklos, Dipannoy Das Gupta
abstract: Template-based crystal structure prediction (CSP) transfers a known crystal structure to a new composition by element substitution, so its accuracy depends on retrieving suitable templates, mapping elements and ranking the resulting candidates correctly. Auditing the original TCSP2.0 implementation on the T180 benchmark, we found that 469 of its 2,347 selected structures (20%) have the wrong composition, caused by element mappings that ignore stoichiometric coefficients and by sequential text substitution that cascades or corrupts element symbols. We propose TCSP3.0, which enforces coefficient-preserving mappings, substitutes species simultaneously on parsed structures and validates every candidate's composition and cell. It further adds periodic-number retrieval, soft oxidation-state evidence, radius-compatibility scoring, structural deduplication, and ORB-v3 machine-learning-potential relaxation and energy ranking of its candidates, as used by deep generative CSP baselines. TCSP3.0 achieves Top-1 and Top-20 match rates of 72.2% and 90.6% on T180, compared with 28.3% and 45.6% for TCSP2.0, and a Top-20 match rate of 74.0% on a new 800-target benchmark (T800). On T180 it also outperforms PNcsp+ and deep generative models CrystalFlow and MaskGXT (Top-1 72.2% versus at most 63.9%). Even without relaxation, TCSP3.0 reaches 67.8% at Top-1 and 90.6% at Top-20 in a median of 28 s per target on two CPU cores, about ten times faster than CrystalFlow. Paired ten-arm ablations on T180 and T800 show that most of the improvement comes from the correctness fixes; structural deduplication significantly improves the Top-5 match rate, embedding-based retrieval is required for coverage, and the remaining scoring features have small or null effects.

infographic.key_insight: TCSP3.0 substantially improves template-based crystal structure prediction, with most gains coming from fixing composition errors rather than adding scoring complexity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Composition-safe template reuse offers an efficient route to candidate crystal structures, reaching 67.8% Top-1 accuracy without relaxation at a median 28 seconds per target on two CPU cores.
method: Enforce coefficient-preserving element mappings, substitute species simultaneously on parsed structures, and validate composition and cell.
Combine embedding-based and periodic-number retrieval with oxidation-state evidence, radius compatibility, and structural deduplication.
Relax and rank candidates using the ORB-v3 machine-learning potential.
infographic.evidence_signal: On T180, TCSP3.0 achieves 72.2% Top-1 and 90.6% Top-20 match rates versus TCSP2.0's 28.3% and 45.6%; Top-20 reaches 74.0% on T800, with paired ten-arm ablations supporting the importance of correctness fixes.
infographic.watch_item: Prediction remains dependent on suitable template coverage; ablations indicate embedding-based retrieval is necessary, while several added scoring features have small or null effects.
infographic.paper_title: TCSP3.0: Template-Based Crystal Structure Prediction with Coefficient-Preserving Element Substitution and Structural Diversity

title: High-efficiency solid-state electrochemical thermal switching through phonon engineering of 2D materials
authors: Harry Mclean, Steven Paul Hepplestone
abstract: Reversible solid-state thermal switches with large thermal contrasts remain rare, yet are essential for advanced thermal management. Using universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) and density functional theory (DFT), we screen 57 transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), spanning the 1T and 2H phases with Li and Mg intercalation. Among the candidates, Li$_a$ZrS$_2$ combines exceptional thermal conductivity switching with low heat capacity. Lithiation to Li$_{0.125}$ZrS$_2$ reduces the cross-plane thermal conductivity from approximately 3.7 to 0.05 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The switching behaviour exceeds that of previously reported solid-state electrochemical thermal switches. Device-level modelling further demonstrates the potential for waste-heat recovery, with a pulsed system capturing 86\% of the energy recovered by an ideal switch. We attribute the switching behaviour to substantial softening of the Zr--Zr framework, with the mean force constant decreasing from approximately 4.2 to 1.2 eV $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}^{-2}$, alongside enhanced scattering of heat-carrying acoustic phonons. These findings establish electrochemical intercalation as a promising route to engineering thermal transport in layered materials.

infographic.key_insight: AI-guided screening identifies Li-intercalated ZrS₂ as a promising thermal switch, with lithiation sharply reducing cross-plane heat transport through framework softening and enhanced phonon scattering.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electrochemically controlled thermal switching could enable adaptive thermal management and pulsed waste-heat recovery.
method: Screen 57 TMDC candidates using universal machine-learned interatomic potentials and DFT.
Evaluate 1T and 2H phases with Li and Mg intercalation.
Analyze phonon transport and model device-level waste-heat recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations predict that Li₀.₁₂₅ZrS₂ lowers cross-plane thermal conductivity from approximately 3.7 to 0.05 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (~74-fold contrast); device modelling reaches 86% of an ideal switch’s recovered energy.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation is needed to establish switching speed, cycling stability, and practical intercalation control.
infographic.paper_title: High-efficiency solid-state electrochemical thermal switching through phonon engineering of 2D materials

title: Precursor Ratio-Controlled Chloride Vacancies in Lead-Free KCuCl3-x Memristors for Forming-Free Gradual Resistive Switching and Neuromorphic Learning
authors: Chinmayee Mandar Mhaskar, Sangeeta Roy Chaudhuri, Ayan Roy Chaudhuri
abstract: Defect engineering of memristive materials offers a powerful strategy for regulating ionic transport and analog resistive switching required for neuromorphic computing. Here, we report a wet chemical synthesis route for chloride-vacancy (VCl) engineering in lead-free all-inorganic KCuCl3-x thin films and establish a direct correlation between defect concentration, electronic structure, transport dynamics, and neuromorphic performance. Controlled precursor-ratio variation systematically tunes the VCl concentration in KCuCl3-x thin films, driving preferential vacancy formation at the terminal chloride sites, band-gap narrowing, and enhanced electronic disorder. W/KCuCl3-x/FTO memristors exhibit stable bipolar VCM-type resistive switching, with increasing VCl concentration promoting forming-free operation. An optimal VCl concentration (~ 1.3*10^21 cm^-3) provides a balance between ionic mobility and defect controllability, resulting in highly linear potentiation/depression characteristics and superior pulse endurance (>104 cycles). When the experimentally measured conductance characteristics of the optimized memristor are implemented as synaptic weights in artificial neural network simulations, recognition accuracies of 98.96% and 91.82% are achieved on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets, respectively. These findings establish precursor ratio-controlled VCl engineering as an effective strategy for simultaneously optimizing ionic transport, analog switching, and neuromorphic learning in lead-free halide perovskite memristors, providing a general materials design principle for energy-efficient neuromorphic electronics.

infographic.key_insight: Precursor-ratio control of chloride vacancies in lead-free KCuCl3-x enables forming-free, gradual resistive switching and highly linear synaptic updates at an optimized defect concentration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Defect-controlled wet chemical synthesis offers a materials-design route to memristors for neuromorphic electronics.
method: Vary precursor ratios to tune chloride-vacancy concentration in KCuCl3-x thin films.
Evaluate electronic structure, transport, and switching in W/KCuCl3-x/FTO devices.
Use measured conductance characteristics as synaptic weights in neural-network simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: At an optimal vacancy concentration of approximately 1.3 × 10^21 cm^-3, the devices show highly linear potentiation/depression and pulse endurance above 10^4 cycles; simulations achieve 98.96% MNIST and 91.82% Fashion-MNIST accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Recognition results are simulation-based; array-scale hardware accuracy and device-to-device uniformity are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Precursor Ratio-Controlled Chloride Vacancies in Lead-Free KCuCl3-x Memristors for Forming-Free Gradual Resistive Switching and Neuromorphic Learning

title: Optimised growth of epitaxial D019 Mn3Ge(0001) thin films via single target sputtering
authors: Servet Ozdemir, Ping-Luen Ho, Callum Brennan-Rich, Matthew Rogers, Philippa Shepley, Ahmet Yagmur
abstract: Materials with chemical identity Mn3X, where X is Sn, Ga, or Ge, are Heusler alloys with intriguing properties that are fundamentally and technologically interesting. They have topological properties with a non-trivial band structure that identify them as Weyl semimetals in the bulk. Their magnetic properties, which give rise to the topological band structure through spin-orbit coupling, are determined by their Kagome lattice structure, making them chiral non-collinear antiferromagnets. Among these materials, Mn3Ge is particularly interesting because it has a larger Berry curvature, leading to a large anomalous Hall conductivity and motivating potential spintronic applications. The desirable properties are only obtained when Mn3Ge has the D019 crystal structure, so producing an easily reproducible growth recipe is the main objective of this paper. Here we show that ultra-high-quality thin films of Mn3Ge with D019 symmetry can be grown from a Mn5Ge target on an Al2O3(0001) substrate with a Ru(0001) seed layer. The expected non-collinear antiferromagnetic order was confirmed by the finding of weak zero-field magnetisation (0.0086 +/- 0.0002) mu_B/Mn that does not saturate at high magnetic fields and has a Neel temperature of (291 +/- 2) K.

infographic.key_insight: Single-target sputtering produces high-quality epitaxial D0₁₉ Mn₃Ge(0001) thin films, the crystal phase needed for its sought-after topological and magnetic properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This growth route supports Mn₃Ge thin-film development for potential spintronic devices exploiting Berry curvature and anomalous Hall conductivity.
method: Sputter from a single Mn₅Ge target.
Grow on Al₂O₃(0001) with a Ru(0001) seed layer.
Evaluate magnetic behavior for consistency with non-collinear antiferromagnetic order.
infographic.evidence_signal: The films showed weak zero-field magnetisation of (0.0086 ± 0.0002) μB/Mn, no saturation at high magnetic fields, and a Néel temperature of (291 ± 2) K.
infographic.watch_item: The Néel temperature near room temperature makes thermal stability an important concern for device operation.
infographic.paper_title: Optimised growth of epitaxial D019 Mn3Ge(0001) thin films via single target sputtering

title: Autonomous atomistic-continuum coupling through uncertainty-aware active learning
authors: Daniel Abdulah, Hariswaran Sitaraman, Ross E. Larsen, Kevin Patrick Griffin, Grace Wei, Janelle Domantay
abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling approach for coupling an atomistic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) surface-chemistry solver with a continuum multi-species fluid dynamics solver across disparate physical length and time scales. The surrogate model predicts boundary mass fluxes for six species and their uncertainties, which the continuum solver monitors to automatically trigger additional KMC simulations when new training data are needed. This enables efficient multiscale coupling and maintains a user-specified level of accuracy. We demonstrate the approach for reactive halide-perovskite vapor deposition, which involves a multi-species vapor jet impinging on a reactive substrate. The KMC solver uses a DFT-calibrated energetics model that we construct as part of this work and provides net deposition and desorption rates for six species. With a conservative uncertainty threshold, the surrogate-coupled approach reproduces cumulative mass fluxes of the directly coupled approach with errors typically within 10-20%, while capturing the non-monotonic dependence of net deposition on species partial pressure. Importantly, the results show that detailed crystal structure need not be explicitly represented to predict quantities exchanged between atomistic and continuum solvers; species-resolved mass fluxes provide a sufficiently low-dimensional representation of the atomistic response. For this accuracy target, the autonomous online-learning approach reduces the number of required atomistic simulations by two to three orders of magnitude relative to direct multiscale coupling.

infographic.key_insight: Uncertainty-aware active learning couples atomistic surface chemistry to continuum flow using six species-resolved mass fluxes, without explicitly representing detailed crystal structure in the exchanged quantities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes multiscale simulation of reactive halide-perovskite vapor deposition more efficient while targeting user-specified accuracy.
method: Generate surface deposition and desorption rates with a DFT-calibrated kinetic Monte Carlo solver.
Train a surrogate to predict boundary mass fluxes and uncertainties for six species.
Trigger additional atomistic simulations when uncertainty exceeds a chosen threshold.
infographic.evidence_signal: For vapor deposition, a conservative uncertainty threshold yielded cumulative mass-flux errors typically within 10–20% of direct coupling, captured non-monotonic pressure dependence, and reduced atomistic simulations by two to three orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertainty thresholds require careful calibration; the reported accuracy and simulation savings are demonstrated for the studied deposition system, not established across other chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous atomistic-continuum coupling through uncertainty-aware active learning

title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density
authors: Arseniy S. Burov, Nadezhda A. Ashikhmina, Nurlan Zhanabayev, Anton O. Boev, Aleksandra D. Radina, Ilya V. Chepkasov
abstract: Sluggish vacancy-mediated self-diffusion in lithium metal limits the critical current density (CCD) of Li anodes in solid-state batteries by promoting interfacial void formation during stripping. To enhance the effective vacancy concentration while preserving the bcc Li host, we screen 50 substitutional solutes using density functional theory (DFT) within a funnel based on automatic phase diagram construction, solution energies, solute-vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits. Using an adaptation of the Lomer model for the dilute limit, we show that only Ag, Ge, and Cd solid solutions are predicted to reach $1~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ within their solubility limits. The thermodynamically estimated CCD of Ag at $\sim 9$ at.% reaches $\sim 4~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ at a theoretical capacity of $1522~\mathrm{mAh~g^{-1}}$. Migration barrier calculations indicate that the enhancement may be partially offset by vacancy trapping, necessitating further validation via molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, Hume-Rothery rules alone prove insufficient as prefilters, whereas machine-learning models trained on the DFT data can eliminate most unsuitable solutes early in the funnel and extend the workflow to related solid-solution searches.

infographic.key_insight: DFT screening predicts that Ag, Ge, and Cd additions can enhance vacancy-mediated transport in bcc Li enough to reach a critical current density of 1 mA cm⁻² within their solubility limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes could reduce stripping-induced interfacial void formation and enable higher-current solid-state batteries.
method: Screen 50 substitutional solutes using DFT phase diagrams, solution energies, vacancy binding, and experimental solubility limits.
Estimate critical current density with a dilute-limit adaptation of the Lomer model.
Assess migration barriers and train machine-learning models to reject unsuitable solutes early.
infographic.evidence_signal: The thermodynamic model predicts approximately 4 mA cm⁻² for Li–Ag at approximately 9 at.% Ag, with a theoretical capacity of 1522 mAh g⁻¹.
infographic.watch_item: Vacancy trapping may partially offset the predicted enhancement; molecular dynamics validation is still needed.
infographic.paper_title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density

title: Methyl radicals dynamics on (100)--(2x1):H diamond surfaces based on refined variational transition state calculations of gas-surface reaction rate coefficients
authors: Emerick Y. Guillaume, Luc Henrard, Ken Haenen, Danny E. P. Vanpoucke
abstract: Theoretical modelling of diamond growth should ideally provide estimates of the growth rate depending on experimental conditions. To that end, a description of all possible reactions related to the competing adsorption, desorption and migration mechanisms is required. Here, we provide precise calculations of the reaction rate coefficient of methyl-related reactions on hydrogen-terminated (100) diamond surface, as $\mathrm{CH_3}$ is known to be the main growth precursor in chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth of diamond. To achieve this goal, we successfully combined Density Functional Theory (DFT) and variational transition state theory (VTST), allowing to extend our analysis to barrierless reaction. Our rigorous treatment of the quasi-free rotation of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ adsorbates on the surface allows us to overcome numerical errors for the finite difference calculations of the vibrational spectra for evaluating the partition functions of the system. Our results suggest that the mechanism that deplete the $\mathrm{CH_3}$ concentration the most is the absorption on a surface radical site. We also evidence the anisotropy of $\mathrm{CH_3}$ migration along the dimer of the (100)-(2x1):H surface. In a more general perspective, the calculated reaction rates coefficient for methyl reactions and migration presented in this work, together with the data for hydrogen reaction and other main gas surface reactions, bridge the gap between the atomic-scale description and the large-scale modelling of diamond growth.

infographic.key_insight: Calculated reaction rates identify methyl adsorption at surface radical sites as the strongest methyl-depletion pathway and reveal direction-dependent migration on hydrogen-terminated diamond.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These rate coefficients help connect atomic-scale surface chemistry to larger-scale models of chemical vapor deposition diamond growth.
method: Combine density functional theory with variational transition state theory.
Calculate methyl adsorption, desorption and migration rates, including barrierless reactions.
Treat quasi-free methyl rotation explicitly to improve vibrational partition functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical rate calculations for the (100)-(2×1):H diamond surface support dominant radical-site adsorption and anisotropic methyl migration; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Predicting overall growth rates requires additional hydrogen and other gas–surface reaction data; this study uses physics-based calculations, not AI.
infographic.paper_title: Methyl radicals dynamics on (100)--(2x1):H diamond surfaces based on refined variational transition state calculations of gas-surface reaction rate coefficients

title: Why Emission Spectral Profile of Diverse Fluoro-phores Look Alike with Thick Polymer Overlayers?
authors: Vinayak Kumar Tiwari, Srishti Batra, Aranyak Sarkar, Vinu Namboodiri, Ravindra Venka-tramani, Manoj Kumbhakar
abstract: Fluorescence from fluorophore-polymer overlayers reflects an interplay between molecular photo-physics and thickness dependent optical propagation. Combining spectrally resolved single mole-cule measurements, transition dipole moment orientation analysis and ensemble fluorescence, we show that structurally and photophysically distinct fluorophores can exhibit similar red shifted emission profiles under thick polymer overlayers even without additional reflecting surface. This similarity indicates a common optical transfer function imposed by the overlayer rather than a pure-ly fluorophore specific molecular response. Although local molecular interactions, excited state dy-namics and vibronic coupling govern intrinsic emission, the overlayer modifies detected spectra through refractive index contrast, dielectric boundary reflections, cavity effects and collection ge-ometry. Vibronic energy spacing distributions remain largely preserved as thickness changes, whereas spectral positions and relative intensities vary systematically. Thus, polymer thickness pri-marily reshapes detected spectrum through optical propagation and outcoupling while retaining vi-brational modes. Time dependent density functional theory identifies candidate Franck-Condon and Herzberg-Teller active dye modes contributing to spectral fluctuations and dipole reorientation.

infographic.key_insight: Thick polymer overlayers can make distinct fluorophores exhibit similar red-shifted emission profiles by reshaping detected light through a common optical transfer function.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Polymer-coated fluorescence devices should account for overlayer thickness and collection geometry when interpreting spectra or designing optical readout.
method: Spectrally resolved single-molecule and ensemble fluorescence measurements
Transition dipole moment orientation analysis
Time-dependent density functional theory of candidate dye vibrational modes
infographic.evidence_signal: Across changing overlayer thickness, spectral positions and relative intensities vary systematically while vibronic energy-spacing distributions remain largely preserved.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract gives no quantitative thickness thresholds or material-specific transfer functions, limiting direct translation to device design.
infographic.paper_title: Why Emission Spectral Profile of Diverse Fluoro-phores Look Alike with Thick Polymer Overlayers?

title: Investigation of the Microstructural and Magnetic Properties of Ni on GeSn Layers
authors: Tharundev V, Dushyant Singh, Subha Maity, Vigneshwari S R, Dhammapriy Gayakwad, Shivesh Yadav
abstract: Thermal processing of nickel (Ni) layers on germanium-tin (GeSn) can strongly modify the Ni film and the Ni/GeSn interface within a restricted thermal budget; however, the influence of GeSn crystalline quality on Ni-Ge-Sn interfacial evolution and the magnetic response of the Ni layer remains incompletely understood. Here, Ni (15~nm)/Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$/Ge/Gd$_2$O$_3$/Si(111) heterostructures ($x = 0.08$ and $0.10$) were investigated following rapid thermal annealing at 573 and 973~K for 10~s using X-ray diffraction, pole-figure analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy depth profiling, and temperature- and field-dependent magnetization measurements. Annealing at 573~K preserves the crystallographic texture of Ge$_{0.92}$Sn$_{0.08}$, whereas Ge$_{0.90}$Sn$_{0.10}$ exhibits microtwin formation and reduced structural integrity. Annealing at 973~K, employed as a severe upper-bound thermal reference, causes extensive structural degradation in both heterostructures, with substantially greater deterioration in the higher-Sn sample. XPS depth profiling reveals progressive Ni-Ge-Sn intermixing accompanied by pronounced Sn surface segregation with increasing annealing temperature. Magnetization measurements show coexisting ferromagnetic and superparamagnetic contributions in the as-deposited and 573~K samples, whereas annealing at 973~K strongly suppresses the ferromagnetic response, producing highly unsaturated $M(H)$ loops together with reduced saturation magnetization and coercivity. These magnetic changes are consistent with extensive interfacial alloying and dilution of the metallic Ni layer. This study establishes a direct correlation between GeSn crystalline quality, interfacial diffusion, and magnetic behavior.

infographic.key_insight: GeSn crystalline quality and annealing temperature govern Ni–Ge–Sn intermixing and magnetic behavior, with higher Sn content associated with greater structural degradation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ni/GeSn integration requires careful thermal-budget control to preserve crystalline quality and limit interfacial alloying that weakens Ni ferromagnetism.
method: Studied 15 nm Ni on GeSn heterostructures with 8% and 10% Sn, annealed at 573 and 973 K for 10 s.
Probed crystal structure and intermixing using X-ray diffraction, pole figures, and XPS depth profiling.
Measured temperature- and field-dependent magnetization.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 573 K, 8% Sn GeSn retained its texture while 10% Sn developed microtwins; at 973 K, both structures degraded and showed strongly suppressed ferromagnetic response.
infographic.watch_item: The 973 K treatment is a severe upper-bound reference, and two compositions and annealing temperatures do not establish a complete processing window.
infographic.paper_title: Investigation of the Microstructural and Magnetic Properties of Ni on GeSn Layers

title: Impact of organic spacer cations on the light and thermal stability of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites
authors: Mahesh Eledath-Changarath, Jesús Ortiga-Fibla, Andrés F. Gualdrón-Reyes, Jesús Rodríguez-Romero, Iván Mora-Seró, Ana Cros
abstract: Long-term stability remains a critical challenge limiting the photovoltaic and optoelectronic applications of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites. In these materials, the choice of the organic spacer plays a key role not only in enhancing environmental stability, but also in determining their structural characteristics and carrier dynamics. Here, we present an environmental photo- and thermal-stability analysis of BA2PbI4 and PEA2PbI4 two-dimensional lead halide perovskites by means of confocal micro-Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy techniques. We have investigated two different organic spacers, n-butylammonium (BA) and 2-phenylethylammonium (PEA), which provide comparable room-temperature luminescence in freshly exfoliated perovskite nanoflakes and degrade similarly through the removal of organic components and fast crystal phase decomposition into PbI2 and Pb0. However, we observed that the PEA organic cation significantly improves crystal morphology and suppresses lattice defects, resulting in slower degradation and enhanced resistance to light and thermal stress under ambient conditions. Our findings indicate that structural and chemical engineering, along with surface passivation and encapsulation strategies, are essential for achieving long-term stability in two-dimensional halide perovskite devices. Nevertheless, optimizing the balance between stability and device performance remains a critical consideration.

infographic.key_insight: The PEA organic spacer improves crystal morphology and suppresses lattice defects, slowing degradation relative to BA in two-dimensional lead iodide perovskites under ambient light and thermal stress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spacer selection can improve perovskite durability, but long-term device stability also requires structural and chemical engineering, surface passivation, and encapsulation.
method: Compared BA2PbI4 and PEA2PbI4 perovskites with different organic spacers.
Assessed ambient photo- and thermal stability using confocal micro-Raman spectroscopy.
Used X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to investigate chemical degradation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Freshly exfoliated nanoflakes showed comparable room-temperature luminescence, while PEA-based crystals degraded more slowly despite both materials losing organic components and decomposing into PbI2 and metallic Pb.
infographic.watch_item: Improved material stability does not establish long-term device durability; the stability–performance trade-off remains unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of organic spacer cations on the light and thermal stability of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites

title: Interpretable Brain Age Prediction Using White Matter Fiber Orientation Distributions with Rotation-Equivariant Deep Learning
authors: Chenyang Fan, Robert D. Sanders, Elie Matar, Yixuan Yuan, Xiang Li, Sharon L. Naismith
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) provides information about white matter microstructure that can support brain age prediction. However, many existing prediction models use diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) scalar metrics that omit orientation information. Deep learning is increasingly used for brain age prediction, but conventional CNNs do not explicitly respect the geometric structure of orientation-dependent features. We present an interpretable brain age prediction framework that combines white matter fiber orientation distributions (WM-FODs) with an SE(3) (Special Euclidean group in 3 dimensions) equivariant CNN. The network operates directly on spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients of the FOD, preserving their transformation properties under rotation. Evaluation in 692 participants aged 36-90 years from the Human Connectome Project Aging dataset showed that the combined framework outperformed the evaluated DTI-based models and conventional CNNs. Averaging predictions from five cross-validation models yielded a mean absolute error of 3.54 years and Pearson's correlation of 0.958. Our results indicated that the performance advantage depended on combining WM-FODs with equivariant processing. Prediction accuracy was highest at a maximum SH order of Lmax = 2 and declined at higher orders. Tract-level occlusion, where each segmented tract was masked in turn, revealed age-dependent patterns of model sensitivity, with importance peaks in frontal projection pathways at 36-44 years, the fornix at 45-54 years, the callosal isthmus at 55-64 years, the middle cerebellar peduncle at 65-74 years, and the callosal genu at 75-90 years. These findings support rotation-equivariant processing of WM-FODs for accurate brain age prediction with anatomically interpretable model sensitivity.

infographic.key_insight: Combining white matter fiber orientation distributions with rotation-equivariant deep learning improved brain age prediction while revealing age-dependent anatomical sensitivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For biomedical imaging systems, respecting the rotational geometry of orientation-dependent features can improve predictive performance over scalar inputs and conventional CNNs.
method: Represent diffusion MRI white matter fiber orientations using spherical harmonic coefficients.
Process coefficients with an SE(3)-equivariant CNN that preserves their transformation properties under rotation.
Mask individual white matter tracts to assess age-dependent model sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 692 HCP Aging participants aged 36–90, averaging predictions from five cross-validation models achieved 3.54-year MAE and Pearson r = 0.958, outperforming evaluated DTI-based models and conventional CNNs.
infographic.watch_item: External-cohort validation is not reported in the abstract, and accuracy declined above the best-performing spherical harmonic order, Lmax = 2.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable Brain Age Prediction Using White Matter Fiber Orientation Distributions with Rotation-Equivariant Deep Learning

title: Role of site-specific coordination for the structural and electronic properties of a Co-HATCN network on silver
authors: Martin Anstett, Ariyan Tavakoli, Simone Mearini, Yan Yan Grisan Qiu, Vitaliy Feyer, Peter Puschnig
abstract: Two-dimensional metal-organic porous networks (2DMOPNs) on metal surfaces provide a versatile platform for exploring emergent electronic and magnetic phenomena in designed surface nanostructures. While the porous architecture is governed by coordination between molecular building blocks and metal centers, most 2DMOPNs utilize only one type of coordination site, leaving the impact of multiple coordination sites largely unexplored. We address this question by investigating the structural formation of a Co-coordinated 2DMOPN on Ag(111) with the linker molecule hexaazatriphenylene-hexacarbonitrile (HATCN), which has two chemically distinct nitrogen coordination sites at the peripheral nitrile groups and pyrazine-type core nitrogen atoms. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) reveals the transformation from a simple honeycomb HATCN structure to a Co-coordinated porous network with three structurally and electronically inequivalent molecules in a 6:3:1 ratio. The existence of two distinct coordination sites leads to selective Co coordination geometries for all three molecules, accompanied by site-specific charge transfer from Co into the former lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), as revealed by momentum-resolved photoemission and density functional theory. Our results demonstrate that site-selective Co coordination not only controls the overall architecture of the porous network structure but also strongly influences the local electronic properties through site-specific metal-molecule interaction, providing a route to tailor the site-specific electronic structure of 2DMOPNs at the molecular level.

infographic.key_insight: Two distinct nitrogen coordination sites in HATCN enable a Co-coordinated porous network on Ag(111) with three inequivalent molecular environments and site-specific electronic properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Selective metal coordination offers a route to tailor porous surface architectures and local electronic structure at the molecular level.
method: STM imaging of HATCN network restructuring upon Co coordination.
Momentum-resolved photoemission to probe electronic states.
Density functional theory to interpret coordination and charge transfer.
infographic.evidence_signal: STM reveals three structurally and electronically inequivalent molecules in a 6:3:1 ratio, while photoemission and DFT identify site-specific charge transfer from Co into the former HATCN LUMO.
infographic.watch_item: The findings concern Co–HATCN on Ag(111); transferability to other substrates or device conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Role of site-specific coordination for the structural and electronic properties of a Co-HATCN network on silver
